messages.author: 3eff71ed43d30ce2
messages.subject: Survey design question
parts:
Hi all,

Just a question on survey design. We're trying to compare abundance estimates for nocturnal mammals through two different survey methods. One was equivalent to a point survey with thermal imaging where observations at each point were recorded over 5 mins, whereas the second method involved observations made over several hours at a singular fixed observation point.

We are deriving abundance from the model summary and multiplying it by area seen from observation point as directed by the Point transect density estimation help section. We are finding that abundances through the second method are considerably higher than those through the first but they align closer to the suspected true abundance for this area. 

Do you think it is possible to directly compare these methods using the Distance package or is our second method (direct observation) not comparable? We are worried that using the point transect function for direct observations is falsely increasing our species abundance through not considering null observations and increased survey effort time? 

We are mostly concerned about whether statistical comparison of these two survey methods  is possible and we are happy to answer any follow up questions RE our data/survey if that helps.

Many thanks for your help,

Gemma Crossan and Emily Currie

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: {Suspected Spam} [distance-sampling] Survey design question
parts:
Gemma, you don’t clarify how you estimate abundance from your second method.  By ‘singular fixed observation point’, do you mean an attempt at a complete count of animals from a point that gives you a view of the whole area of interest?  i.e. a vantage point count?  But you then apply a detection function to correct that count?  I am not clear how that would work.  Point transect methods cannot be applied when you record for several hours from a point, as animal movement will generate substantial upward bias in any abundance estimate.  And the method needs a design with a number of points – you cannot get valid inference if you have a single observation point.  You say the second method agrees better with suspected true abundance, but that may simply be because suspected true abundance is also inflated, depending on how the suspicion came about!

 

If the point transect method is underestimating abundance, then you need to carefully consider the assumptions.  You don’t give any details to know whether issues like responsive movement away from observers, non-random selection of points, or failure to detect animals very close to a point could be occurring.

 

Steve Buckland

parts:
Hi Stephen,

Many thanks for your reply. Effectively the second method is a ''vantage point count' as you said, which, during analysis we treated as a point transect; in total we had 4 non-random observation points and recorded over several hours for 7 consecutive nights. Yes, we then fitted a detection function model to this data but we are uncertain that the normal assumptions of distance sampling can be applied to this survey method. 

Our first survey method was a point transect (thermal observations), points were selected at regular intervals along a track so not truly random and there were issues with view shed potentially preventing detection of animals close to the point so this could account for the lower abundance estimate from this method.

We are essentially trying to establish the most efficient method for estimating badger density in an area of mixed pasture and woodland. The point transect method would seem to be the most robust method but has a lot of practical drawbacks when conducted in rough terrain at night. We would therefore like to compare it with the 'vantage point count' method however we are uncertain how best to calculate abundance from this method for comparison.

Please let us know if you would require any more information,

Gemma and Emily

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: {Suspected Spam} [distance-sampling] Survey design question
parts:
Gemma

Thanks for replying to Steve's request for further details. Your vantage point counts suffer from positive bias arising from animal movement. As duration of a count increases, animals in the course of their affairs, will move. Random movement causes positive bias in estimates because animals that move toward the vantage point will be included in the detections while animals moving away are less likely to be detected. This has been demonstrated by Glennie et al. (2015)
  • Glennie, R., Buckland, S. T., and Thomas, L. (2015), The Effect of Animal Movement on Line Transect Estimates of Abundance, PLoS One, 10, e0121333

Regarding your thermal point transect surveys. You note the detections were made along tracks and badgers are either attracted or repelled by the tracks. In either event, badgers know where the point transects are located hence distribution of badgers with respect to the thermal detector is being confounded with the estimated shape of the detection function.

One of our colleagues developed a method to disentangle the two distributions when conducting point counts along roads (in your neck of the woods).
  • Marques, T. A., Buckland, S. T., Borchers, D. L., Tosh, D., & McDonald, R. A. (2010). Point transect sampling along linear features. Biometrics, 66, 1247–1255. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01381.x

but it requires the collection of additional data and there is no "off-the-shelf" software to conduct such an analysis.

I'm afraid that doesn't exactly resolve your problems, but it does highlight the difficulties of the issue.

messages.subject: Re: {Suspected Spam} [distance-sampling] Survey design question
parts:
You might want to consider using camera-trap distance sampling. You then don’t need to navigate woodland at night, and you are likely to get more detections. In this method, you can leave cameras out for long periods, as it uses a variation of point transect sampling so that animal movement doesn’t bias estimates - unless that movement is in response to cameras. See Howe et al., 2017, Methods in Ecology and Evolution.
Steve
